We like to think in terms of if we just put in more work, we will get more results. Uh the problem is when we're dealing with muscle fibers, it doesn't doesn't scale that way. The quality of the work matters. Okay? And you can't sustain a high quality of work for very long. You just simply can't. You can only do so much of it. Uh and and I think people don't understand if you think in terms of, you know, if you go over and you're trying to, you know, shovel a bunch of rocks, small rocks with a shovel out of a out of a big pile, coming in and just doing more work isn't going to necessarily move more rocks. So, think of it in the [clears throat] terms of when we're trying to recruit muscle fibers. Uh, and think in terms of quality reps, effective reps that get the upper threshold muscle fibers, right? The fastest switch fibers because that's where most of our growth is going to occur. Um, and hopefully people understand that the longer you train, the less and less and less that you get from uh more intermediate type fibers. When you're a novice, they grow a lot. The longer you train, we come down to, you know, once you've been training a few years, pretty much nearly 100%. It's not 100%, but it's it's well past 90%. All your muscle growth is only coming from those those fast twitch fibers. And so really, the only thing that stimulates those is reps really close to failure or truly maximum effort work. All right? and they can only be recruited so many times so often. So in other words, you know, people will use stuff like effective reps. It's like, well, if you leave three reps in reserve, you got two effective reps, but if you did two sets to failure, you got 10. That's working off the concept that the last five, which is not a proven theory, um that the last five or so out of each set before failure are the effective reps. Well, if you're getting 10 of them from two sets to failure and maybe a little more if you try to do a hair rest pause or something, but that's, you know, we could debate how much that is, right? Versus uh well, if I just left three reps in the tank, I'd need five sets to get them. See where we're going with that? The problem is is that we can only recruit them so often. Okay? You can only recruit them so often. So if you just keep adding more and more work, people are like, "Well, I get weaker and weaker. I can't perform later with the same muscles, with the same performance that I performed with uh early in the workout, right? Because you're not getting all those those fast twitch fibers anymore. They're too fatigued." Okay? They're [snorts] too fatigued. This is why even if we're going to train sometimes multiple muscle groups, it makes a little sense to space stuff to get a little higher quality sets. Like let's say you're doing, you know, even even if it's not a full body, you're doing your chest and your back in the same workout, right? You may want to do a chest exercise, then a back exercise before your next chest exercise. Why? Well, because you're going to get a little higher quality work because you've kind of worked those opposing muscle groups. You've given longer to rest. All right? And when we just stack more and more volume, we're just simply not getting enough rest. I'm not saying it doesn't cause any growth, but we're what I'm saying is it's it's very very little potentially compared to the the beating up your recovery. So when you think of it in terms of this, especially if you think in terms of the effective reps, um it makes more sense that hey, leaving a few reps in the tank, you will need five total sets to get the same stimulus that you would have got from two sets to failure. And if you start just taking numerous sets to failure and you're not able to replicate performance very effectively, you're not getting any effective reps. You know, again, we're back over to are some maybe a few of those intermediate fibers maybe growing a little. Sure, but they're very, very little growth stimulus again. And they're going to eventually kind of cap out more and more anyways over the years. So, ultimately, our focus if you're really trying to maximize your gains needs to be to get the muscle fibers that are going to have the most growth potential. So, we come back over to more isn't necessarily better. better is better, right? Understand that you were doing it almost as interval training like uh highintensity interval training type cardio. You're not really stimulating muscle growth from it, right? So it's it's not what we are thinking of, hey, the benefits of weight training. Am I gaining muscle? Well, no. But it's also a hell of a lot harder to recover from when you're doing everything that way. So if you're going to do stuff like that, your recovery has to be even more on point because otherwise it starts interfering with your growth, starts interfering with your strength, interfering with your quality of life. But again, the thing I will always point out, it's about the the total amount of quality work that you have done in a session, in a week, in a month that matters, not how much work you did. Okay? It's not how much work you did, it's how much of it was actually high quality that was challenging to all the muscle fibers, right? Particularly the ones that we are trying to grow, which is ultimately going to be mostly the fast twitch at the end of the day. And that will become every year that you train that is going to skew more and more and more in that direction. Okay? And that's just the way that it is. So again, focus on quality over quantity. Reps in reserve is killing your gains. Hey everybody, it's Jason Blah here. I thought I would chat with you guys about this today. Here's some things that you have to consider. Uh it's generally accepted even by researchers and scientists that the closer you get to muscle failure, the more muscle growth you get on a set for set basis. There are some, and this is controversial and not proven with evidence. There's PhDs in the field who do say that the closer you get to failure, the more valuable each rep gets. Okay? In other words, thinking in terms of effective reps, the rep right before failure probably is slightly slightly more effective than the rep was three reps before failure, even though both cause growth. And I don't mean on a set for set basis. I mean the actual individual rep because it's closer to maxing out all of your possible muscle fibers to the point where they can't fire anymore. Right? Do we all understand this? The reason we need multiple hard reps to usually get a muscle fiber as fatigued as we want. Otherwise, we could just do one rep maxes and all get really jacked, right? So, we do need a certain number of repetitions. We need multiple repetitions. Closer you get to failure, the more valuable each of those reps probably is, maybe is. But we know set for set. All right, let's say you have a weight you can do 10 reps and you will fail on rep 11. If you do eight reps, you know that you're getting less growth than 10 reps from that same set. There's less training stimulus, not even subject to debate. Okay? Because if if we're going to argue effective reps, you're just going to have less total effective reps, right? You you could have pulled off 10, but you stopped at eight. Now, a 10 rep max for eight reps will still cause muscle growth, but it's not as high of a quality. And that's the point we're making here with this, right? Because if if muscle fibers had if everything had to go to failure, the the main muscle on an exercise to get any growth, then we could throw out this idea of, you know, the big compounds causing multiple muscles to grow. But we know that they do, right? It's just only one muscle probably fails. And when form starts to break, it's because that muscle did fail and something else is trying to take over. Compensatory strength. Okay? Which is one reason why it's really beneficial in big compounds to go a hair beyond technical failure, but can stop short of of total failure because you did have a muscle that failed. If technique breaks down, you reached muscle failure on at least one muscle. Okay? All right. So, we all understand this. If everyone gets this, I think we're good. If you don't, then we got a problem. If if you don't realize doing 10 reps with your 10 rep max will cause a larger training response than eight reps with your 10 rep max, just, you know, two reps in reserve versus zero in reserve, okay? But still not still not absolute failure. If you don't understand this and we got a problem, right? So then you don't actually believe that you know multiple repetitions are really necessary in any way. Uh but over over to the point, well that sounds good. So people are like, "Okay, so we can just leave reps in reserve. Won't be as exhausted." Well, here's the problem. So that's that progressive tension needs to come in the form of adding reps or adding weight because even the adding the reps, you're reaching other new muscle fibers that are getting fatigued that were not getting fatigued early in the set. And as long as you're doing more work, you're getting tension onto onto additional muscle fibers. Even the ones that have previously grown, once they've grown, it's now easier to do that same weight and reps. So, if you're not adding something to the workload, they're not restimulating. They're not being put into a position to where they have to grow. So, it really is a matter of performance. That is what we are talking about. Subjecting the muscles to a higher workload, making them perform more so that they continue to adapt.

So what does that tell you? That most of your strength is going to come from size. Okay. At the level of the tendon it's almost guaranteed. So what then what are we dealing with with other differences? Difference in leverages differences in coordination. So, so a lot of interuscular coordination, extra muscular coordination, a lot of that is skill. We call skill. That is what we mean. Finding the right technique, levers and learning to coordinate everything to where your muscles all kind of fire in the order and pattern that you want them to to move the weight through that pattern that you're trying to do. There's a skill to that. That's why practicing lifting heavy is a skill. Okay? And all that skill and stuff accounts for a relatively small percentage compared to the amount of muscle mass that a person has.

The body temperature will go up. If you're not careful, you would just excrete heat. You will sweat to cool back down, right? And goes up, fidgeting goes up. So, in these sort of situations, the amount of fidgeting and extra moving that people do burns hundreds of calories. in addition to hundreds and hundreds of extra calories just burning off as thermic effect. This is what happens. Now, people say, "Oh, well, so you must be burning through body fat." Well, no, you're not. You're not burning. Your metabolic rates going through the roof, but because you're you're only burning all that glucose and then burning it off as excess heat, your body has no need to burn body fat in that in that scenario anymore. It has no need to burn dietary fat. So you store most of the fat that you eat at that point. Very straightforward.
